Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes based on all the material gathered.

---

# 1 Thessalonians 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1: *"So when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left on our own in Athens."*

- **Paul's sacrificial love.** Paul chose to be left "alone" in Athens — a vast, idolatrous metropolis — rather than keep Timothy with him. This self-denial for the sake of the Thessalonians' spiritual welfare demonstrates the depth of his pastoral affection (Enduring Word / David Guzik). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **"Could bear it no longer"** translates the Greek verb *stego*, which originally meant to keep water out (like a watertight vessel or roof) and came to mean "to endure" or "contain." Paul's suspense about how the young church was faring under persecution became intolerable — he could no longer "hold it in" (Precept Austin, citing Hiebert, Bruce, Vine). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_31-3]
- **"We thought it best"** (*eudokeo*) conveys not grudging consent but a free, deliberate choice — Paul was "well pleased" to pay this cost for their sake (Precept Austin, citing Keathley). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_31-3]
- **Historical difficulty with Acts.** Ellicott notes the apparent tension with Acts 17:15–16 / 18:5: from Acts it seems Silas and Timothy never joined Paul in Athens at all. Ellicott's preferred solution is that Silas and Timothy *did* join Paul briefly at Athens and were then almost immediately sent back into Macedonia — Silas to Berea or Philippi, Timothy to Thessalonica. This explains Paul being "left alone" and also how in Acts 18:5 both men later come to Corinth from Macedonia. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **Catholic reading (Haydock):** Paul was "not being able to be at rest, for not seeing you, nor hearing concerning you." He sent Timothy because he could not bear to remain uninformed of their constancy. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 2: *"We sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith."*

- **Twofold mission — establish, then encourage.** Paul wanted Timothy to do two things: to *establish* (strengthen, make firm) and to *encourage* (comfort, exhort) the Thessalonians. Establishing comes first; encouragement can only really help once someone is set in the right direction (Enduring Word / Guzik). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Timothy's titles.** Paul calls Timothy "our brother" (stressing equality in the family of God) and "God's fellow worker" (stressing his labor in the gospel). The Pulpit Commentary notes these titles "help to honor him before the Churches, and to challenge the abiding confidence of the Thessalonians." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **Textual variant.** Ellicott notes that many of the best editors judge the traditional "minister of God" (KJV) to be an interpolation. The preferred reading is "our brother, and God's fellow-worker in the gospel of Christ." Timothy was well known in Thessalonica, yet Paul particularises him — possibly because Timothy was the letter-bearer and Paul wished the church to give him due deference despite his youth. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **"Minister" (where retained) means servant.** The Greek *diakonos* originally denoted a table waiter and came to signify lowly service of any kind; it stresses the *activity* of serving, not an official title (Enduring Word, citing Hiebert and Morris). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- Gill adds that Timothy's work of "establishing" — though ultimately God's work — is usually done through the ministry of the Word, and this is the very purpose of gospel ministry to the churches. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/3.htm]

---

## v. 3: *"so that none of you would be shaken by these trials. For you know that we are destined for this."*

- **"Shaken" (*sainesthai*).** The ancient Greek word originally described a dog wagging its tail. John Trapp (cited by Guzik) explains: "Flattered, as a dog flattereth, by moving his tail; the devil, by flattering you, with promise of more ease by a contrary course, will but do as a dirty dog, defile you with fawning." Satan flatters believers with promises of an easier path to lure them from faith (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **"Destined for this" / "appointed to this."** Affliction is not a sign of God's anger but part of the normal Christian life. God appoints affliction to teach perseverance, obedience, how to comfort others, and deeper fellowship with Jesus — just as suffering taught Jesus (Hebrews 2:10; 5:8). The symbol of Christianity is the cross, not a feather bed (Enduring Word, citing Morgan). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Two Greek words for suffering.** Guzik notes that neither *thlipsis* (physical pain, emotional hardship, suffering under temptation) nor *pasko* (physical sufferings, hardships generally) is used exclusively for persecution. Affliction is broader than persecution only. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Catholic reading (Haydock, citing Witham):** "That we are appointed thereunto. That is, meet with trials and troubles in this world, as our Saviour Christ foretold." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-thessalonians-3.html]
- Precept Austin provides the Greek *keimetha* (we are appointed / set / destined), emphasising that this is God's sovereign placement. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_31-3]

---

## v. 4: *"Indeed, when we were with you, we kept warning you that we would suffer persecution; and as you know, it has come to pass."*

- **Forewarned is forearmed.** Paul used the imperfect tense of *prolego* ("we kept on telling you beforehand"), meaning he warned them *repeatedly*, not just once. Though he was only with them a few weeks, he made the place of suffering in Christian life a core teaching (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Jesus' pattern.** Paul followed Christ's own example, who forewarned His disciples so they would not stumble: "These things I have spoken to you, that you may be kept from stumbling" (John 16:1). To leave converts unwarned about suffering is to do them a serious injustice (Precept Austin, citing Hiebert). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_34-5]
- **"We would suffer tribulation."** Guzik points to Jesus' parable of the soils (Matthew 13): Jesus said *when* tribulation arises, not *if*. The testing of faith is inevitable. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **The verb *thlibo* (suffer affliction).** Literally means to press, squeeze, crush, or hem in. Vincent notes it derives from *tribulum*, the Roman threshing-roller. Trials are a "squeeze play" — compression produces gold, and compression produces character (Precept Austin, citing Richison). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_34-5]

---

## v. 5: *"For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and caused our labor to be in vain."*

- **Paul switches to "I."** The shift from "we" in v.1 to "I" here indicates Paul's personal, individual anguish and sense of urgency (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **"The tempter" — Satan.** Satan, as in Job's case, wanted to exploit the season of suffering to make the Thessalonians give up on God. Orchard's Catholic Commentary concisely notes: "'The Tempter' is Satan; cf. Matthew 4:3." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/1-thessalonians-3.html]
- **"Our labor might be in vain."** If the Thessalonians withered under affliction, Paul's work would be like the seed in Jesus' parable that fell on rocky ground — it sprang up quickly but withered under the sun of trials. Paul took practical action (sending Timothy) rather than merely worrying (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Paul's depressed state.** Precept Austin (citing Hiebert) notes that Paul's "subdued missionary activities at Corinth before the return of Silas and Timothy (Acts 18:5) seems to indicate that Paul was deeply depressed because of the heavy burden of suspense." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_34-5]
- **Dispensational reading (Gaebelein):** Paul's anxiety was not only pastoral but eschatological — he was thinking of the day of Christ "when the servant receives the reward and the saints are 'the crown of glorying.'" If the tempter succeeded, Paul would lose that crown. He cites 1 John 2:28 in support. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 6: *"But just now, Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news about your faith, your love, and the fond memories you have preserved, longing to see us just as we long to see you."*

- **"Good news" — gospel language.** The verb used here (*euangelizomai*) is the normal NT word for "preach the gospel." This is the *only* place in all Paul's writings where it is used in a non-gospel sense — Timothy "gospeled" good news to Paul about the Thessalonians (Enduring Word, citing Morris). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **"Faith and love."** Calvin is cited: "In these two words he states concisely the sum total of godliness. All who aim at this double mark are beyond the danger of error for the whole of their life." (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Faith = confidence in God to endure; love = mutual tenderness.** Ellicott explains: faith enabled them to endure trials; love was the tenderness with which they helped one another through. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **"Fond memories" / "good remembrance."** The Thessalonians had not believed the false rumours about Paul; they still cherished him and longed to see him. This was a deep relief to Paul (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Timothy's movements.** Precept Austin notes that Timothy returned to Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:5), not at Athens, meaning Paul had moved on from Athens by the time Timothy came back. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_36-8]

---

## v. 7: *"For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and persecution, we have been reassured about you, because of your faith."*

- **Paul's own affliction.** Paul wrote from Corinth, where he described his state as "in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling" (1 Cor 2:3). The Greek pair *anagke kai thlipsei* ("distress and affliction") covers both inward pressure and outward crushing (Precept Austin). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_36-8]
- **Comfort flowed from *their* faith.** Paul was comforted not by his own circumstances but by news of the Thessalonians' steadfastness. "The good news from the Thessalonians refreshed his spirit and filled him with new energy" (Gaebelein). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 8: *"For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord."*

- **"For now we live."** This is dramatic language. Paul felt that his very life depended on their steadfastness. Spurgeon is quoted: "Never is the servant of God so full of delight as when he sees that the Holy Spirit is visiting his hearers… On the other hand, if God does not bless the word of his servants it is like death to them." (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Calvin** (cited by Enduring Word) notes: "All pastors are reminded by this of the kind of relationship which ought to exist between them and the church. When things go well with the Church, they are to count themselves happy, even though in other respects they are surrounded by much distress." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Catholic reading (Haydock, citing Witham):** "We live… in joy and comfort, if you stand firm in the faith of Christ." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 9: *"How can we adequately thank God for you in return for our great joy over you in His presence?"*

- **Overflowing thanks.** Paul sees the Thessalonians' steadfastness as a gift from God that he cannot adequately repay with thanksgiving. His joy is "in His presence" — lived consciously before God (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Spiritual prosperity, not material.** Guzik notes that some find it easy to rejoice in others' material prosperity; Paul honestly rejoiced in their *spiritual* prosperity. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]

---

## v. 10: *"Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking from your faith."*

- **"Night and day praying exceedingly."** The Greek behind "exceedingly" (*huperekperissou*) is a double compound — "probably the most emphatic of all" ways to express abundance (Enduring Word, citing Morris). Paul's prayer was intense, constant, and overflowing. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **"Supply what is lacking."** Despite all his compliments (1 Thess 1:3, 1:7, 2:13, 2:19–20, 3:6), Paul honestly acknowledged their faith was incomplete. He believed his *personal presence* would do what letters could not. Matthew Poole (cited by Guzik): "Though his Epistles might avail towards it, yet his personal presence would do more. There is a peculiar blessing that attends oral preaching, more than reading." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Catholic reading (Orchard):** What was lacking was their "catechetical instruction so abruptly broken off" when Paul had to flee Thessalonica (cf. Acts 17:5). Timothy's report was favourable, but the Thessalonians still needed fuller teaching. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/1-thessalonians-3.html]
- **Haydock (Catholic):** "It is by preaching that the faith of Jesus Christ and true religion are both begun and accomplished." Letters help, but face-to-face teaching is primary. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 11: *"Now may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you."*

- **Unity of Father and Son.** The Greek verb "direct" (*kateuthunai*) is singular, though the subject is compound: "our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus." This grammatical feature strongly implies the unity of the Godhead. Hiebert calls the construction "a devout prayer-wish" that "approaches the language of prayer and is virtually a prayer" (Enduring Word, citing Thomas). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** "It is a striking proof of the unity of the Father and Son." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-thessalonians-3.html]
- **Orchard's Catholic Commentary** makes the identical point: "'direct': this verb is singular in the Greek, thus showing that the two Persons, Father and Son, share the same divine nature." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/1-thessalonians-3.html]
- **Paul's motive.** Despite the encouraging report, Paul believed the Thessalonians still needed apostolic authority and teaching. The church is "founded upon the apostles, with Christ Himself the chief cornerstone" (Eph 2:20). That apostolic ministry is now preserved in the New Testament (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]

---

## v. 12: *"And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows."*

- **"Increase and abound."** Ellicott notes that "increase" points to progress and "abound" to the state that progress reaches — "Multiply you in love until you have enough and to spare of it." The love is to extend outward: "so that you may not only love one another abundantly, but all mankind — missionary efforts being the supreme work of Christian love." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **Love as the mark of discipleship.** Guzik cites John 13:35 and 1 John 4:20 to show that love is the essential identifying mark of Christians. Love begins in the family of God but must go beyond — Jesus said our love is small if we only love those who love us (Matt 5:46–47) (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Paul as standard of love.** Paul daringly set *himself* as the standard: "just as our love for you overflows." Guzik comments: "We should live such Christian lives that we could tell young Christians, 'Love other people just the way that I do.'" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-3/]
- **Catholic reading (Haydock):** "And may the Lord multiply you. That is, increase the number of Christians among you." This represents a different interpretive tradition — reading the increase quantitatively (more converts) rather than qualitatively (growth in love). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-thessalonians-3.html]

---

## v. 13: *"so that He may establish your hearts in blamelessness and holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints. Amen."*

### Traditional / widely shared readings:

- **Love is the means; holiness is the goal.** Ellicott sketches the chain of thought beautifully: growing and overflowing love toward mankind is the *means* by which God establishes hearts in blameless holiness. Love is the "bond of perfectness" (cf. Col 3:14). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]
- **"Hearts" (*kardia*)** refers to the whole inner person — "the thinking, willing, and feeling dimensions of human existence" (Constable, citing Wanamaker). Holiness must be inward, not merely external. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]
- **"Blameless"** means free from any reasonable charge or accusation, not sinless perfection. It is blamelessness *before God*, who sees the heart (Barnes, Gill). [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]
- **"At the coming" (*parousia*).** This is the third reference to Christ's coming in the letter (cf. 1:10; 2:19). Paul's eschatology is intensely practical: the thought of Christ's return motivates holy living here and now. As Barnes puts it: "As we are to appear before him, we should so live that our Judge will find nothing in us to be blamed." [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

### Interpretive differences on "with all His saints":

This is the most debated phrase in the chapter. Who are "the saints" (*hagioi*) who accompany Christ at His coming?

- **Reformed / Calvinist (Calvin):** Christ will come "with all his saints." Calvin takes the phrase to mean the holy ones who accompany Christ, and he sees it as an admonition that "we are called by Christ for this end — that we may be gathered with all his saints." He also stresses that our holiness is always imperfect and mingled with pollutions; it is only by remission of sins that it bears God's eye. Completion awaits the coming of Christ. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Presbyterian (Barnes):** "Saints" includes both the holy angels (Matt 25:31) and all the redeemed who will surround Christ. The idea is that before that vast holy assembly, we should be prepared to appear blameless. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Baptist / Calvinist (Gill):** "Saints" means either holy angels, or "rather the souls of his people, whom he will bring with him, and will raise their dead bodies, and reunite them to their souls." At that point they shall be unblamable in holiness, both in soul and body. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Methodist / Arminian (Clarke):** Clarke's focus is not on identifying the saints but on love as the source of holiness: "Without love to God and man, there can be no establishment in the religion of Christ… he who is filled with love is unblamable in holiness." He also applies the "coming" individually: "When thy soul departs from thy body it will be the coming of the Lord to thee." [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Wesley's Notes (Methodist):** Wesley's note is brief: "With all his, Christ's, saints — Both…" (the excerpt cuts off, but the note indicates Wesley included both angels and redeemed believers). [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Dispensational (Gaebelein):** Gaebelein distinguishes sharply: this is Christ coming *with* His saints (the day of His manifestation in glory), not coming *for* His saints (the Rapture). This is "another phase" of His coming — when Christ is manifested, the saints are manifested with Him in glory (cf. Col 3:4; 2 Thess 1:10). The coming "for" His saints is taught in 1 Thess 4:13–18; the coming "with" them is taught here. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-thessalonians-3.html]

- **Dispensational (Constable):** Notes that *parousia* can refer to the Rapture, the actual arrival, or what follows. Here Paul's concern is the believers' readiness to give a good account at the judgment seat of Christ. "The saints who will join the Thessalonians before the judgment seat of Christ include all other Christians (cf. 2 Cor 5:10; 2 Thess 1:10) and perhaps angels." [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

- **Anglican / Ellicott:** Ellicott leans toward the view that "saints" here means holy *men* (not angels), because the Greek "seems almost to indicate that these 'saints' are to be assessors in the judgment — an honour to be given only to holy men" (cf. Luke 22:30; 1 Cor 6:3). He anticipates Paul's teaching in 1 Thess 4:14. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/3.htm]

- **Catholic (Orchard):** "The saints: probably the angels, cf. Zech 14:5; Matthew 25:31; the souls of the just do not seem to be included under the term here." The focus is on preparation for the Last Judgment, "of which the Particular Judgment at the hour of death is in a sense merely the anticipation." The "Amen" is noted as "possibly a liturgical addition." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/1-thessalonians-3.html]

- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** Rejects any notion that Paul taught an "imminent soon-coming." He argues that the Thessalonians got that impression "from their dull understanding, not from any statement Paul had made to that effect," because otherwise Paul could not have written 2 Thessalonians to correct them. On "saints," he concludes it is safest to include *both* angels and redeemed, based on 1 Thess 4:14 and 2 Thess 1:7. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/3-13.html]

---

## Summary of Key Denominational Distinctives

| Issue | View |
|---|---|
| **"With all His saints" — angels only?** | Catholic (Orchard): yes, probably angels. |
| **"With all His saints" — redeemed only?** | Ellicott (Anglican): yes, holy men as assessors in judgment. Gill (Baptist): rather the souls of His people. |
| **"With all His saints" — both angels and redeemed?** | Barnes (Presbyterian), Coffman (Restoration), Constable (Dispensational), Wesley (Methodist) — the majority view across traditions. |
| **Coming "with" vs. "for" His saints** | Dispensational (Gaebelein): distinguishes two phases — the Rapture (coming *for* saints, 1 Thess 4) and the Revelation (coming *with* saints, 1 Thess 3:13). |
| **"Multiply you" (v.12) — quantitative or qualitative?** | Haydock (Catholic): increase the number of Christians. Most Protestant commentators: increase in love. |
| **The singular verb in v.11** | Noted across traditions (Catholic, Dispensational, Reformed) as evidence of the unity of Father and Son. |
| **Particular Judgment at death** | Catholic (Orchard): the Particular Judgment at death anticipates the Last Judgment. Clarke (Methodist) similarly: "When thy soul departs… it will be the coming of the Lord to thee." |

---

*Sources used: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin (with Hiebert, Morris, Bruce, Vine, Richison, Keathley, Spurgeon), Ellicott's Commentary, Gill's Exposition, Pulpit Commentary, Calvin's Commentary, Barnes' Notes, Clarke's Commentary, Wesley's Notes, Coffman's Commentaries, Constable's Expository Notes, Gaebelein's Annotated Bible, Orchard's Catholic Commentary, Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary.*
